role: Main figure 1: response to payoff incentives
title: Cooperation frequency across normalized payoffs
caption: Each panel shows one model in isolated, simultaneous self-play. We normalize payoffs to R=1 and P=0, varying S horizontally and T vertically on a 13×13 grid with spacing 0.25. Color is the fraction of individual C choices, averaged within valid joint games: yellow means all observed choices were C and purple means all were D. C and D are analytical labels; prompts used neutral A/B labels, reversed across two blocks. Each cell contains at most two valid games (four decisions). Dashed/red regime boundaries at S=0 and T=1 separate dominance, coordination, and anti-coordination regions. The clearer own-payoff presentation was an exploratory follow-up. Here “susceptibility” means observed response to payoff incentives, not a safety or manipulation score. Most cells are not strict Prisoner’s Dilemma; strict PD occupies S<0, T>1.

role: Main figure 2: observed minus theoretical switching thresholds
title: Threshold displacement under each model’s reported opponent beliefs
caption: Each row is one model. Left: vary normalized T at fixed S, looking for a C-majority to D-majority switch. Right: vary S at fixed T, looking for a D-majority to C-majority switch. The vertical axis is observed threshold minus theoretical threshold, in normalized payoff units. At each payoff cell we use the same valid decisions and reported beliefs for both curves. Observed C frequency comes from the actual actions. The theoretical curve is the fraction of best-response C choices implied by each decision’s own reported q, using Δ=q(1−T)+(1−q)S. Exact utility ties permit either action, so theory can give a range of C frequencies. Beliefs can change from cell to cell; this is a conditional best-response comparison, not a unique Nash-equilibrium prediction. For each curve, a single crossing is bracketed by the last decisive majority on one side and the first decisive majority on the other. Intermediate observed 50% frequencies and theoretically ambiguous majorities widen the bracket. If observed and theoretical brackets are [Lo,Uo] and [Lt,Ut], the displacement bar is [Lo−Ut,Uo−Lt]. No midpoint is presented as an estimated threshold. Gray ranges include zero; orange ranges exclude zero at this grid resolution. This is not a statistical significance test. Arrows show one-sided displacement bounds conditional on a single-switch continuation. A × above a panel marks multiple or reversed crossings; ○ marks an unresolved comparison. There are 47 two-sided comparisons, 16 one-sided bounds, 14 multiple/reversed cases, and 27 unresolved cases among 104 slices. Each cell has at most four matched decisions (2,702 in total); slices reuse cells and are not independent. The 0.25 grid gives descriptive crossing brackets, not confidence intervals or fitted population thresholds. No binary search or additional model calls were used.

title: The theoretical phase space of symmetric two-action games
caption: Positive affine normalization maps payoffs to s=(S−P)/(R−P) and t=(T−P)/(R−P), for R>P. This leaves two degrees of freedom and preserves expected-utility incentives. The map shows twelve strict payoff orderings, regime boundaries, and group-payoff boundaries. The repository’s (5,3,1,0) baseline is at (s,t)=(−0.5,2). It is an analytic reconstruction following Falmagne’s SIAM article; no model calls are involved.

title: Matrix presentation substantially changes apparent cooperation
caption: The targeted exploratory control compares the same strict-PD payoff cells and first two label blocks under row/column wording and explicit “your payoff / opponent payoff” wording. Each bar contains 32 valid decisions per model and role. Qwen’s column-role C frequency changes from 31/32 to 1/32, while its row-role frequency changes from 0/32 to 2/32. The game utilities and individual-payoff objective are identical, but both payoff perspective and display order change. These observations demonstrate presentation sensitivity without isolating its cause. This control motivated the clearer-presentation grid used in figures 1 and 2.
